q: A patient with pressure-like chest discomfort has new horizontal ST depression in several contiguous leads. Which interpretation should guide the nurse’s immediate communication to the provider?
o: The tracing may reflect myocardial ischemia and needs prompt evaluation.
The finding confirms a completed infarction.
The tracing is diagnostic of pericarditis.
The change is expected with uncomplicated sinus tachycardia.
r: ST depression can accompany subendocardial ischemia, but ECG changes alone do not establish the cause or extent. Pair the tracing with symptoms and urgent assessment.

q: A patient being evaluated for acute coronary syndrome has a rising high-sensitivity troponin on serial testing and new ischemic ECG changes. What does the trend most strongly indicate?
o: A chronic, stable elevation unrelated to current symptoms.
Acute myocardial injury in a clinical picture concerning for infarction.
Atrial depolarization without ventricular involvement.
A normal response to exercise that requires no follow-up.
r: A rise or fall in troponin indicates acute myocardial injury; ischemic symptoms and ECG changes support acute MI. Interpret results with timing and the whole presentation.

q: A patient develops sudden chest pressure, diaphoresis, and ST elevation in contiguous leads. What is the nurse’s priority?
o: Wait for the next routine ECG before reporting the change.
Ask the patient to walk to see whether symptoms resolve.
Activate the facility’s acute coronary response and obtain immediate evaluation while maintaining monitoring.
Document the tracing as a normal variant and reassess at the end of the shift.
r: Acute symptoms with new contiguous ST elevation may represent an occlusive MI and require time-critical evaluation; do not delay escalation.

q: A patient with a known narrowed aortic valve reports fainting while climbing stairs. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Encourage faster walking to build cardiac endurance.
Place the patient flat and give an unprescribed fluid bolus.
Reassure the patient that fainting is expected and harmless.
Stop exertion, assess vital signs and perfusion, and promptly report the exertional syncope.
r: Exertional syncope can indicate limited forward flow from aortic stenosis. Stop activity and assess before escalating.

q: A patient with a new apical systolic murmur has worsening breathlessness and crackles. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
o: Pulmonary congestion related to impaired mitral valve function.
Improved left ventricular filling from aortic stenosis.
An isolated conduction delay with no hemodynamic effect.
Reduced pulmonary blood flow from a benign flow murmur.
r: A systolic apical murmur with pulmonary symptoms can reflect mitral regurgitation and elevated left atrial/pulmonary pressures; assess oxygenation and escalate.

q: A patient with suspected aortic stenosis asks why an echocardiogram is needed. Which response is accurate?
o: “It is used only to identify coronary artery blockages.”
“It shows valve structure and how well blood moves through the valve and heart.”
“It replaces the need to assess your symptoms and blood pressure.”
“It measures electrical conduction but not valve function.”
r: Echocardiography evaluates valve anatomy, flow, and ventricular response. It complements, rather than replaces, clinical assessment.

q: A patient with mitral stenosis develops increasing dyspnea when lying flat. Which assessment is the priority?
o: Bowel sounds and abdominal girth only.
Pupil response and visual acuity.
Respiratory status, oxygen saturation, lung sounds, and work of breathing.
Skin turgor on the forearm only.
r: Mitral stenosis can raise left atrial and pulmonary pressures; orthopnea may signal worsening pulmonary congestion.

q: A patient has a harsh systolic murmur radiating toward the neck and diminished peripheral pulses. Which condition best fits this assessment pattern?
o: Mitral stenosis.
Mitral valve prolapse.
Tricuspid regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis.
r: A systolic ejection murmur radiating to the neck with weak pulses is characteristic of aortic outflow obstruction.

q: A patient with valve disease reports new reduced activity tolerance and swelling in both ankles. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess vital signs, oxygenation, weight trend, edema, and signs of heart failure.
Recommend increasing salt intake to improve circulation.
Advise stopping all prescribed cardiac medicines.
Wait several weeks because edema is unrelated to valve disease.
r: Reduced tolerance and edema may indicate worsening cardiac function. Focused assessment informs prompt escalation and treatment decisions.

q: A patient with a mechanical valve is preparing for discharge on long-term anticoagulation. Which statement shows understanding?
o: “Once I feel well, I can stop the anticoagulant.”
“I will keep my follow-up blood tests and contact the care team before changing medicines.”
“I can take any over-the-counter pain medicine without checking.”
“I should double a missed dose whenever I remember.”
r: Mechanical valves generally require ongoing anticoagulation and monitoring. Changes, missed doses, and interacting medications need clinician guidance.

q: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve calls before a dental procedure and asks whether to take antibiotics. What is the best nursing response?
o: “Everyone with a valve must take antibiotics before every dental visit.”
“Antibiotics are never considered for prosthetic valves.”
“Your clinician needs to review the procedure and your valve history to determine whether prophylaxis is indicated.”
“Use leftover antibiotics without contacting the clinic.”
r: Endocarditis prophylaxis recommendations depend on cardiac risk and procedure. Direct the patient to the prescribing team rather than giving a blanket rule.

q: On the first day after valve surgery, the nurse notes increasing shortness of breath, falling blood pressure, and cool extremities. What is the priority?
o: Wait until the scheduled postoperative round.
Encourage oral fluids and ambulation without assessment.
Remove monitoring leads to reduce anxiety.
Immediately alert the surgical/cardiac team and support airway, breathing, circulation while assessing.
r: Acute respiratory and perfusion deterioration after cardiac surgery may signal a serious complication. Escalate immediately and continue close monitoring.

q: A patient with a mechanical valve reports black, tarry stools while taking an anticoagulant. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Seek urgent medical evaluation and do not independently stop or adjust the medication without guidance.
Take an extra anticoagulant dose to prevent valve clotting.
Wait until the next routine appointment.
Treat the stool with an over-the-counter laxative and continue as usual.
r: Melena may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding during anticoagulation. Urgent evaluation is needed; medication changes require clinician direction.

q: A patient after valve replacement asks what symptom should prompt an immediate call. Which response is best?
o: “Only a mild change in appetite matters.”
“Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, or signs of bleeding need prompt attention.”
“A new fever is expected and never needs reporting.”
“A missed anticoagulant dose cannot affect the valve.”
r: Acute cardiopulmonary symptoms, infection signs, and bleeding can indicate important postoperative or anticoagulation complications.

q: A patient with chronic mitral regurgitation develops new orthopnea and oxygen saturation below the prescribed target. What is the nurse’s first response?
o: Place the patient flat and leave to obtain a routine weight.
Encourage a large meal before reassessment.
Sit the patient upright, assess breathing and oxygenation, and activate prompt clinical support.
Delay action until a repeat echocardiogram is available.
r: New hypoxemia and orthopnea can reflect pulmonary congestion. Positioning and prompt assessment/escalation take priority over routine testing.

q: A patient with mitral regurgitation asks why blood may flow backward during ventricular contraction. Which explanation is correct?
o: The aortic valve blocks all blood from leaving the heart.
The right ventricle sends blood directly into the left atrium.
The atria stop contracting during every heartbeat.
The mitral valve does not close effectively, allowing some blood to return to the left atrium.
r: Mitral regurgitation is backward flow through an incompletely closed mitral valve during systole.

q: Which finding in a patient with mitral regurgitation is most concerning for reduced cardiac output?
o: New confusion with cool, clammy skin and a weak pulse.
A stable, soft systolic murmur documented previously.
Warm hands with unchanged activity tolerance.
A regular pulse and no symptoms after usual activity.
r: Altered mentation and cool skin suggest impaired perfusion and require urgent assessment, unlike a stable known murmur alone.

q: A patient with mitral regurgitation is being monitored for pulmonary congestion. Which change is most useful to report promptly?
o: A single unchanged heart sound finding.
Increasing crackles with a rising oxygen requirement.
Improved ability to lie flat.
A stable temperature and appetite.
r: Crackles and increased oxygen need indicate worsening gas exchange, potentially from elevated pulmonary pressures and fluid accumulation.

q: A patient with chronic mitral regurgitation says, “I get more winded doing the same walk I did last month.” What is the best response?
o: Tell the patient that exercise tolerance never relates to valve disease.
Recommend stopping all activity indefinitely without evaluation.
Assess the change in symptoms and notify the clinician because it may reflect progression or heart failure.
Suggest doubling any prescribed diuretic dose.
r: A change from baseline can signal worsening regurgitation or heart failure. It warrants assessment and provider review; patients should not self-adjust medication.

q: A patient with severe mitral regurgitation suddenly develops pink frothy sputum and severe respiratory distress. What should the nurse do?
o: Offer water and reassess in an hour.
Ask the patient to lie flat to conserve energy.
Continue routine documentation before notifying anyone.
Call emergency response, support oxygenation/ventilation, and remain with the patient.
r: Pink frothy sputum with acute distress is consistent with severe pulmonary edema. Immediate emergency response and airway/breathing support are required.

q: Which assessment pattern is most consistent with mitral regurgitation causing left-sided congestion?
o: Dyspnea, crackles, and reduced exercise tolerance.
Isolated unilateral calf pain with normal breathing.
Increased urine output and clear lungs.
Abdominal tenderness without cardiopulmonary changes.
r: Backflow into the left atrium can raise pulmonary venous pressure, causing dyspnea and crackles.

q: A patient with mitral regurgitation is scheduled for echocardiography. Which question is most important for the nurse to clarify beforehand?
o: Whether the patient should stop every medication for a week.
Whether a transesophageal study is planned and whether the patient received fasting/sedation instructions.
Whether the patient must avoid all liquids for 24 hours for any echo.
Whether an ECG is prohibited on the same day.
r: A transthoracic study differs from a transesophageal study; sedation and fasting instructions may apply to the latter and should be confirmed.

q: A patient with known mitral regurgitation has new palpitations and lightheadedness. Which action is appropriate?
o: Assume the symptoms are caused by anxiety without assessment.
Encourage the patient to drive home alone.
Check pulse and vital signs, obtain/maintain cardiac monitoring as indicated, and report the new symptoms.
Wait for the next annual visit.
r: New palpitations with lightheadedness may reflect dysrhythmia or compromised perfusion and should be evaluated promptly.

q: A patient with mitral regurgitation asks why the care team tracks daily weight. Which explanation is best?
o: “Weight tells us whether the valve has healed.”
“Daily weight replaces checking for breathing changes.”
“Weight is used only to decide whether you may eat.”
“A rapid increase can be an early clue that fluid is accumulating.”
r: Daily weights help detect fluid retention and worsening heart failure when measured consistently; symptoms and other findings still matter.

q: A young adult recovering from a viral illness reports chest discomfort, unusual fatigue, and a racing heartbeat. What is the safest nursing advice?
o: Avoid strenuous activity and seek prompt clinical assessment for possible cardiac involvement.
Resume intense training to test cardiac endurance.
Use an energy drink and wait several days.
Ignore the symptoms because myocarditis occurs only in older adults.
r: Myocarditis can follow infection and present with chest symptoms, fatigue, or arrhythmia. Restrict exertion pending evaluation.

q: A patient being evaluated for myocarditis develops sustained ventricular tachycardia and becomes unresponsive. What is the priority?
o: Obtain a routine temperature before acting.
Activate emergency response and begin the facility’s resuscitation protocol.
Ask the patient to cough and bear down.
Wait for troponin results to confirm myocarditis.
r: Unresponsiveness with a dangerous ventricular rhythm is an immediate resuscitation emergency; do not wait for diagnostic confirmation.

q: Which finding in a patient with suspected myocarditis warrants the most urgent escalation?
o: Mild fatigue with stable vital signs.
A low-grade temperature with no cardiac symptoms.
New hypotension with worsening dyspnea and altered mentation.
A remote history of uncomplicated viral illness.
r: Hypotension, respiratory compromise, and altered mentation suggest hemodynamic deterioration and possible heart failure or shock.

q: A patient with suspected myocarditis asks why the clinician ordered an ECG and cardiac biomarkers. Which response is most accurate?
o: “Either test alone proves myocarditis.”
“They measure only lung function.”
“Normal results would always exclude every cardiac problem.”
“They help assess electrical changes and evidence of heart muscle injury, but results are interpreted together with your symptoms and other tests.”
r: ECG and biomarkers contribute evidence but are not individually definitive. The diagnosis uses the full clinical evaluation.

q: A patient diagnosed with myocarditis asks when to return to competitive sports. What should the nurse say?
o: “Wait for your cardiology team to clear you; strenuous activity may need to be restricted during recovery.”
“Return as soon as the fever resolves.”
“Exercise through chest pain to rebuild the heart.”
“Sports are permanently prohibited for everyone with myocarditis.”
r: Active myocardial inflammation can increase arrhythmia risk with exertion. Return-to-activity decisions require individualized medical clearance.

q: A patient with a prosthetic valve has fever and chills. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Reassure the patient that fever is unrelated to a valve.
Promptly notify the clinician and anticipate evaluation for bloodstream infection and endocarditis.
Recommend waiting one week to see if it resolves.
Use leftover antibiotics before any cultures are collected.
r: Fever in a patient with a prosthetic valve is concerning for infection. Timely assessment is essential; cultures should not be compromised by unsupervised antibiotics.

q: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis has blood cultures ordered before the first antimicrobial dose. Why is this sequence important?
o: Cultures prevent all antibiotic adverse effects.
Antibiotics cannot work unless cultures are positive.
Cultures can help identify the organism and guide targeted treatment.
Blood cultures determine the patient’s valve size.
r: Collecting ordered cultures before antimicrobials when clinically feasible improves the chance of identifying the causative organism; urgent care should not be delayed in unstable patients.

q: A patient receiving treatment for endocarditis suddenly develops facial droop and difficulty speaking. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give oral fluids and reassess later.
Wait for the next antibiotic dose.
Encourage the patient to sleep.
Activate the stroke response and document the time symptoms were first noted.
r: Endocarditis can cause embolic events. New focal neurologic deficits require immediate stroke evaluation and precise last-known-well documentation.

q: A child with a known ventricular septal defect develops increased work of breathing and poor feeding. What should the nurse do?
o: Assess oxygenation and perfusion promptly and report possible worsening heart failure.
Assume this is a normal feature of every VSD.
Delay evaluation until the next routine visit.
Encourage prolonged feeding without rest breaks.
r: Poor feeding and respiratory effort can signal increased cardiac workload or heart failure in a child with a shunt.

q: A caregiver asks how a ventricular septal defect can increase pulmonary blood flow. Which explanation is accurate?
o: Blood flows from the pulmonary artery directly into the aorta through the defect.
Blood can pass from the higher-pressure left ventricle through the opening into the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation.
The defect prevents any blood from entering the lungs.
The opening is between the atria, not the ventricles.
r: A VSD may allow left-to-right flow because left ventricular pressure is higher, increasing pulmonary circulation depending on defect size and resistance.

q: A nurse is assessing an infant with a VSD. Which change is most important to trend over time?
o: Hair color and eye color.
Number of wet diapers without any intake context.
Feeding endurance, respiratory effort, growth, and signs of fluid overload.
Whether the infant startles to a loud sound.
r: Feeding and growth can reveal the sustained energy cost of cardiac disease; respiratory and fluid status help identify heart failure.

q: A patient with sharp chest pain reports that it worsens when lying flat and improves when leaning forward. Which nursing action is appropriate?
o: Label the pain as reflux without further assessment.
Encourage the patient to lie flat and exercise.
Withhold all evaluation because positional pain is benign.
Assess vital signs and ECG findings and promptly report the pattern for evaluation.
r: Positional pleuritic chest pain can occur with pericarditis, but acute chest pain requires assessment to distinguish serious causes.

q: A patient with pericarditis suddenly becomes hypotensive, restless, and increasingly short of breath; neck veins appear distended. What complication should the nurse suspect?
o: Cardiac tamponade from impaired filling.
Uncomplicated sinus bradycardia.
Aortic stenosis.
Chronic stable mitral regurgitation.
r: Hypotension, distress, and venous distention can indicate tamponade, where pericardial pressure limits cardiac filling. This is an emergency.

q: A patient being treated for pericarditis reports increasing chest pain and new faintness. What is the best nursing response?
o: Tell the patient to wait until pain medicine is due.
Reassess promptly for hemodynamic change and escalate the new symptoms.
Encourage unassisted ambulation.
Document the symptoms as expected without assessment.
r: Worsening pain with presyncope can signal progression or hemodynamic compromise; reassessment and escalation are warranted.

q: A patient with acute pericarditis asks why the pain changes with position. Which explanation is most appropriate?
o: “The pain proves that a coronary artery is completely blocked.”
“It means the heart has stopped contracting.”
“Inflammation around the heart can make movement and contact with nearby structures painful.”
“Position changes cause the valve leaflets to detach.”
r: Pericardial inflammation often causes pleuritic, positional pain. It is not by itself proof of coronary occlusion or valve failure.

q: A patient with pericarditis is discharged with instructions to seek care for which symptom?
o: A brief, unchanged mild ache that improves as instructed.
A single episode of hiccups.
Mild thirst after a walk.
Increasing shortness of breath, fainting, or rapidly worsening chest discomfort.
r: Dyspnea, syncope, and worsening pain may signal effusion or tamponade and require prompt evaluation.

q: A patient with a known pericardial effusion develops falling blood pressure, muffled heart sounds, and tachycardia. What is the priority?
o: Escalate immediately for possible tamponade and support circulation while monitoring.
Schedule routine follow-up for next month.
Encourage oral fluids and leave the patient alone.
Administer an unprescribed diuretic.
r: Effusion with hypotension, tachycardia, and muffled sounds suggests tamponade. Rapid intervention may be lifesaving.

q: A patient with a moderate effusion asks why the team is monitoring blood pressure and breathing so closely. Which response is best?
o: “The fluid always strengthens each heartbeat.”
“Fluid around the heart can sometimes restrict filling and reduce the amount of blood pumped.”
“Monitoring is only needed to check for pneumonia.”
“An effusion affects the lungs but cannot affect circulation.”
r: A growing effusion can impair diastolic filling and cardiac output; close monitoring detects tamponade physiology.

q: During assessment of a patient with pericardial effusion, which trend is most concerning?
o: Stable blood pressure and unchanged breathing.
Improved urine output with warm extremities.
Progressive tachycardia with narrowing pulse pressure and worsening perfusion.
A single normal temperature reading.
r: A compensatory rising heart rate and narrowing pulse pressure with poor perfusion can precede overt tamponade.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a ventricular rate of 160/min, blood pressure 78/46 mm Hg, and new confusion. What intervention should the nurse anticipate urgently?
o: Routine outpatient rate-control follow-up.
A vagal maneuver as the only response.
An unsupervised oral fluid challenge.
Synchronized cardioversion for an unstable tachyarrhythmia, per emergency protocol.
r: Hypotension and altered mentation indicate instability. Emergency rhythm management, often synchronized cardioversion, should not be delayed.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has no symptoms and a stable blood pressure. Which assessment finding is expected?
o: An irregularly irregular pulse.
A regular pulse with identical intervals.
A fixed rate of 60/min in every patient.
A palpable pulse for every atrial depolarization.
r: Atrial fibrillation produces disorganized atrial activity and an irregularly irregular ventricular response unless another rhythm or pacing pattern is present.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation asks why anticoagulation is being discussed even though the heart rate is controlled. What is the best explanation?
o: “Anticoagulants are used only to slow the heart rate.”
“Atrial fibrillation can allow blood to pool and form clots; your stroke risk and bleeding risk guide this decision.”
“A controlled rate means stroke is impossible.”
“Everyone with atrial fibrillation must take the same anticoagulant dose.”
r: Rate control does not eliminate embolic risk. Anticoagulation is individualized using stroke and bleeding risk and shared clinical decision-making.

q: A patient scheduled for elective cardioversion for atrial fibrillation is unsure whether to take the prescribed anticoagulant. What should the nurse advise?
o: Stop it immediately because cardioversion does not involve clot risk.
Double the dose on the morning of the procedure.
Contact the procedural/cardiology team for instructions and do not stop it independently.
Replace it with aspirin without clinician approval.
r: Cardioversion planning considers thromboembolic risk and anticoagulation timing. The patient should follow explicit clinician guidance, not self-adjust.

q: A patient with atrial flutter becomes pale and diaphoretic and reports chest pressure. Blood pressure is falling. What is the nurse’s priority?
o: Ask the patient to walk to improve circulation.
Delay action until the rhythm converts spontaneously.
Offer a meal and repeat vital signs after eating.
Activate emergency support, assess perfusion, and prepare for urgent rhythm management.
r: Chest pressure with falling pressure signals instability. Rapid escalation and monitoring are essential.

q: A patient taking a rate-controlling medicine for atrial fibrillation reports dizziness when standing. What should the nurse do first?
o: Check heart rate and blood pressure, assess symptoms and fall risk, and report concerning findings.
Tell the patient to take an additional dose.
Assume dizziness is unrelated to treatment.
Advise the patient to discontinue all cardiac medicines immediately.
r: Rate-control therapy may contribute to bradycardia or hypotension. Assess before advising changes and reduce fall risk.

q: The monitor shows an irregular rhythm in a patient with atrial fibrillation, but the patient is alert with stable vital signs. Which action is appropriate?
o: Perform unsynchronized defibrillation.
Assess the patient, verify the rhythm and pulse, and follow the prescribed rate-control/monitoring plan.
Ignore the rhythm because atrial fibrillation never causes complications.
Initiate CPR despite a present pulse and stable condition.
r: Treat the patient rather than the monitor. A stable rhythm warrants verification, assessment, and the prescribed plan, not shock or CPR.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation taking an anticoagulant reports a sudden severe headache and weakness on one side. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassure the patient that anticoagulants prevent all strokes.
Give the next anticoagulant dose and wait.
Activate emergency stroke evaluation immediately and note symptom onset/last known well.
Schedule a routine appointment for next week.
r: Focal neurologic symptoms may indicate stroke or intracranial bleeding. Immediate emergency assessment is required.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a resting pulse of 48/min with lightheadedness after a dose of a rate-control drug. What is the best action?
o: Give another dose to prevent a fast rate.
Encourage strenuous exercise to raise the pulse.
Document the pulse as acceptable without checking symptoms.
Assess blood pressure and perfusion, hold further dosing only per protocol/order, and promptly notify the prescriber.
r: Symptomatic bradycardia warrants immediate assessment and prescriber notification. Medication changes follow orders/protocols.

q: A patient with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation asks what to do if palpitations occur at home. Which teaching is safest?
o: Seek urgent help for chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, or stroke symptoms; report sustained new palpitations to the care team.
Ignore every palpitation if a diagnosis is already known.
Take another dose of every heart medicine when symptoms begin.
Drive to the clinic if faint or short of breath.
r: Teach emergency warning signs and avoid unsafe self-dosing or driving when unstable.

q: A patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation asks whether leafy vegetables must be avoided. Which response is best?
o: “Avoid all vegetables permanently.”
“Keep vitamin K intake reasonably consistent and discuss major diet changes with your anticoagulation team.”
“Eat a large amount only on days before blood tests.”
“Diet cannot affect warfarin response.”
r: Vitamin K intake can affect warfarin anticoagulation. Consistency and monitoring are safer than complete avoidance or abrupt changes.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation is scheduled for a transesophageal echocardiogram before cardioversion. What should the nurse verify?
o: That the patient has eaten a large meal immediately beforehand.
That no monitoring is needed after sedation.
Fasting instructions, consent, and post-sedation safety arrangements.
That the patient will drive home after receiving sedation.
r: TEE involves esophageal instrumentation and often sedation; fasting, consent, and safe recovery planning are important.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a rapid ventricular response but remains alert with adequate blood pressure. Which initial goal is likely?
o: Deliver unsynchronized shock regardless of stability.
Suppress all atrial activity with an unprescribed drug.
Discontinue cardiac monitoring because the patient is stable.
Control ventricular rate and assess the cause and symptoms under the prescribed plan.
r: In a stable patient, management commonly focuses on rate control and evaluation. Rhythm strategy depends on the clinical context.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation reports taking an over-the-counter cold remedy and now has a fast heartbeat. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask which product and dose were used, assess vital signs, and contact the clinician/pharmacist about possible interaction.
Recommend taking more of the cold medicine to finish the course.
Assume all nonprescription medicines are safe with cardiac conditions.
Tell the patient to stop prescribed anticoagulation.
r: Some cold products can affect heart rate or blood pressure. Clarify exposure and seek medication guidance without changing essential prescriptions.

q: A nurse is teaching a patient prescribed a direct oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation. Which statement indicates understanding?
o: “I can stop it when I have no palpitations.”
“I will take it as prescribed and call the care team for unusual bleeding or a head injury.”
“I should take a double dose after any missed dose.”
“I do not need to tell other clinicians that I use it.”
r: Anticoagulants reduce clot risk but increase bleeding risk. Adherence, injury reporting, and medication disclosure are important; missed-dose advice is product-specific.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has a new oxygen requirement and crackles. What should the nurse prioritize?
o: Focus only on counting the apical pulse.
Encourage the patient to lie flat.
Assess respiratory distress and perfusion and promptly escalate possible heart failure or ischemia.
Wait for the next scheduled outpatient visit.
r: New pulmonary congestion with a dysrhythmia may reflect decompensation and needs urgent respiratory and cardiac assessment.

q: A patient asks whether a smartwatch rhythm alert proves atrial fibrillation. What response is most accurate?
o: “A watch alert is always a definitive diagnosis.”
“A normal watch reading excludes future atrial fibrillation.”
“The alert means you should take someone else’s medication.”
“It can flag an irregular pattern, but a clinician needs to confirm the rhythm with appropriate ECG recording.”
r: Wearables can prompt evaluation but do not replace diagnostic ECG interpretation or clinical assessment.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and a pulse becomes unresponsive; the monitor shows a pulseless ventricular rhythm. What action is required?
o: Start CPR and follow the pulseless arrest algorithm, including defibrillation if indicated by rhythm.
Attempt elective synchronized cardioversion.
Give oral rate-control medication.
Wait for a cardiologist before starting resuscitation.
r: A pulseless arrest requires immediate CPR and algorithm-based resuscitation; do not delay for consultation.

q: A patient on anticoagulation is scheduled for an invasive procedure and asks whether to skip the next dose. What is the safest response?
o: “Skip every dose for a week.”
“Do not change the dose on your own; the procedural and prescribing teams should give you a coordinated plan.”
“Take extra doses to prevent a clot during the procedure.”
“Replace it with an herbal supplement.”
r: Periprocedural interruption depends on medication, renal function, and procedure bleeding risk. The team must individualize the plan.

q: A patient with atrial flutter has a regular narrow-complex rate near 150/min and is stable. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
o: Ventricular fibrillation is present.
The rhythm is certainly normal sinus rhythm.
Atrial flutter with possible 2:1 AV conduction should be considered and the rhythm confirmed.
A regular rate excludes an atrial dysrhythmia.
r: Flutter with 2:1 conduction can produce a regular ventricular rate around 150/min; inspect the tracing and assess the patient.

q: A stable patient develops a regular narrow-complex tachycardia and remains alert with a palpable pulse. What should the nurse do first?
o: Deliver unsynchronized defibrillation immediately.
Begin chest compressions despite a pulse.
Leave the patient alone to obtain a medication.
Assess hemodynamic stability, obtain/continue ECG monitoring, and follow the ordered SVT protocol.
r: A stable tachycardia with a pulse requires assessment and protocol-based management; electrical therapy depends on instability and rhythm.

q: A patient in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia becomes hypotensive and confused despite initial measures. What intervention should the nurse anticipate?
o: Urgent synchronized cardioversion per emergency protocol.
Routine observation without intervention.
An unsupervised oral dose of a home medicine.
A prolonged walking trial.
r: Instability with tachycardia requires urgent synchronized cardioversion when appropriate; delay risks worsening perfusion.

q: A stable patient with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia is instructed by the clinician to try a vagal maneuver. Which teaching is appropriate?
o: Massage both carotid arteries forcefully without supervision.
Use only the instructed maneuver and stop if severe symptoms occur; never press on the eyes or neck.
Bear down until losing consciousness.
Use a household electrical device to reset the rhythm.
r: Vagal maneuvers may be used in selected stable SVT, but unsafe carotid or ocular pressure must be avoided and symptoms monitored.

q: A patient has sinus tachycardia while febrile and dehydrated. Which approach best addresses the rhythm?
o: Assume the sinus rate itself is the primary disease in every case.
Give a rhythm-control drug without checking the cause.
Identify and treat the underlying cause while monitoring the patient.
Ignore the elevated rate because sinus rhythms cannot be harmful.
r: Sinus tachycardia is often a response to fever, hypovolemia, pain, or hypoxia. Treating the trigger is central.

q: A patient’s telemetry shows sinus bradycardia at 52/min. The patient is alert, normotensive, and denies symptoms. What is the appropriate response?
o: Start CPR because the rate is below 60/min.
Give atropine automatically without an order or symptoms.
Apply defibrillation pads and shock.
Continue assessment and monitoring; correlate the rate with symptoms and baseline.
r: A low rate alone does not establish instability. Assess perfusion, symptoms, medications, and baseline before intervention.

q: A patient with sinus bradycardia is pale, hypotensive, and lightheaded. What should the nurse prioritize?
o: Activate urgent support, assess perfusion, and follow the symptomatic bradycardia protocol.
Reassure the patient that all slow rhythms are harmless.
Encourage the patient to walk unassisted.
Delay intervention until a routine ECG is read.
r: Bradycardia with hypotension and symptoms is unstable and requires prompt protocol-based care.

q: The nurse is reviewing a rhythm strip. Which sequence correctly describes normal cardiac conduction?
o: AV node, ventricles, SA node, atria, His-Purkinje system.
SA node, atria, AV node, His-Purkinje system, ventricles.
Ventricles, atria, AV node, SA node, bundle branches.
Purkinje fibers, SA node, AV node, atria, ventricles.
r: Normal impulse formation begins in the SA node, spreads through the atria, pauses at the AV node, and travels through His-Purkinje pathways to the ventricles.

q: A patient with sinus tachycardia reports sudden pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnea after surgery. What should the nurse do?
o: Assume anxiety is causing the rate and leave the patient alone.
Ask the patient to ambulate to reduce the heart rate.
Treat as an emergency, assess oxygenation and circulation, and escalate possible pulmonary embolism.
Give a dose of a rate-controlling medication without assessment.
r: Sinus tachycardia may be a response to hypoxia or PE. Postoperative pleuritic pain and sudden dyspnea demand urgent evaluation.

q: A patient asks why a 12-lead ECG is obtained during palpitations. Which explanation is correct?
o: “It measures the amount of blood in your lungs.”
“It permanently corrects an irregular rhythm.”
“It tells us the exact cause of every palpitation by itself.”
“It records electrical activity from multiple views and can help identify the rhythm or ischemic changes.”
r: A 12-lead ECG records cardiac electrical activity from multiple leads; it supports but does not independently answer every clinical question.

q: A patient with a regular tachycardia has a pulse and is alert. Before any rhythm intervention, what is the most important check?
o: Whether the patient is stable, including blood pressure, mental status, chest pain, and signs of shock.
Whether the patient has eaten today.
Whether the telemetry alarm can be silenced.
Whether a family member agrees with the monitor.
r: Treatment urgency depends on hemodynamic stability, not only the displayed rate.

q: A patient with a narrow-complex tachycardia has no symptoms and the rate returns to baseline spontaneously. What should the nurse do next?
o: Delete the telemetry record because the rhythm ended.
Document the episode, assess for triggers and symptoms, and notify the care team per plan.
Give a rescue medication that was not prescribed.
Discharge the patient without notifying anyone.
r: Resolution does not remove the need to assess symptoms, triggers, recurrence risk, and prescribed follow-up.

q: A nurse sees a monitor alarm for a fast rate but the patient is talking comfortably. What is the best first step?
o: Silence the alarm permanently.
Administer emergency medication based only on the display.
Assess the patient and verify the rhythm and pulse before acting on the alarm.
Assume the patient is in cardiac arrest.
r: Artifact and monitor errors occur. Correlate the tracing with the patient and a palpable pulse before intervention.

q: A student asks what the P wave represents on an ECG. Which answer is correct?
o: Ventricular depolarization.
Ventricular repolarization.
The period of ventricular relaxation only.
Atrial depolarization.
r: The P wave reflects atrial depolarization; the QRS reflects ventricular depolarization and the T wave ventricular repolarization.

q: A nurse identifies a regular rhythm with a P wave before each QRS and a consistent PR interval. What is the best interpretation if the rate is within the patient’s expected range?
o: Sinus rhythm with coordinated atrioventricular conduction.
Atrial fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation.
Complete heart block.
r: Consistent P-to-QRS relationships and regular intervals support sinus rhythm, interpreted with the rate and clinical context.

q: Telemetry displays a sudden irregular tracing while the patient is moving, but the pulse remains regular. What should the nurse do?
o: Treat the displayed pattern as ventricular fibrillation without checking the patient.
Check electrode contact and obtain a clean tracing while continuing patient assessment.
Remove all monitoring and document an arrhythmia.
Tell the patient not to report symptoms.
r: Movement or poor electrode contact can create artifact. A regular pulse and stable patient call for verification, not reflex treatment.

q: A patient with a chest tube has continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. What should the nurse do first?
o: Clamp the tube routinely for the rest of the shift.
Strip the tubing forcefully toward the drainage unit.
Assess the patient and system for an air leak, checking connections and the insertion site per policy.
Add sterile water to the suction-control chamber without checking the device.
r: Continuous water-seal bubbling may indicate an air leak; assess the patient and system. Routine clamping or stripping can be harmful.

q: A chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the patient’s chest. What is the nurse’s immediate action?
o: Reinsert the used tube into the tract.
Leave the opening uncovered while finding supplies.
Clamp the remaining tubing and walk away.
Apply a sterile occlusive dressing according to facility policy, call for help, and assess breathing.
r: A dislodged tube creates risk of air entry. Protect the site and promptly assess respiratory status while obtaining help.

q: The chest drainage system tips over, but the tubing remains connected and the patient is stable. What should the nurse do?
o: Restore the unit upright, check the water-seal level and connections, then reassess the patient.
Disconnect the tube from the drainage unit and leave it open to air.
Clamp the tube for an extended period.
Raise the drainage unit above chest level.
r: Keep the system upright below chest level and verify function. Avoid routine disconnection or clamping, which can compromise drainage.

q: A patient’s chest tube stops tidaling, and the patient becomes more short of breath. What is the priority?
o: Assume the lung has fully expanded and remove the tube.
Assess respiratory status and the tubing for obstruction or displacement; promptly notify the clinician.
Flush the tube without an order.
Wait until the end of the shift to recheck.
r: Absent tidaling may have more than one explanation, but worsening dyspnea is concerning. Assess the patient and system and escalate.

q: A patient with a chest tube asks why the drainage container must remain below the chest. Which response is correct?
o: “It makes the tube drain faster by gravity into your heart.”
“It prevents every possible infection.”
“Keeping it lower helps prevent drainage or air from flowing back toward your chest.”
“The container’s position does not matter.”
r: The collection system stays below chest level to support drainage and reduce backflow risk.

q: After central-line placement, a patient develops sudden dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, and falling blood pressure. What complication should the nurse suspect?
o: Uncomplicated atelectasis.
Stable pleural effusion.
Chronic bronchitis.
Tension pneumothorax.
r: Acute unilateral loss of breath sounds with respiratory distress and hypotension after a procedure suggests tension physiology and requires emergency response.

q: A patient with blunt chest trauma has paradoxical movement of a chest segment and increasing work of breathing. What is the priority?
o: Support oxygenation, assess ventilation, and urgently escalate possible flail chest.
Apply a tight circumferential chest wrap.
Encourage deep coughing without pain control or assessment.
Leave the patient supine and unmonitored.
r: Paradoxical chest-wall motion suggests flail segment and impaired ventilation. Provide respiratory support and urgent evaluation; tight binding limits expansion.

q: A patient with suspected hemothorax becomes pale and tachycardic after trauma. Which assessment is most urgent?
o: Visual acuity and hearing.
Signs of hemorrhagic shock and respiratory compromise.
Bowel pattern from the prior week.
Skin color at a healed scar.
r: Blood in the pleural space can impair ventilation and cause significant blood loss; assess circulation and breathing rapidly.

q: A patient with a small spontaneous pneumothorax is being observed. Which change requires immediate escalation?
o: Mild soreness at the site with stable vital signs.
A stable oxygen saturation on the ordered support.
Sudden worsening dyspnea with hypotension or tracheal shift.
An unchanged respiratory rate.
r: Worsening distress and hemodynamic compromise can indicate tension pneumothorax, an emergency.

q: A patient has a penetrating chest injury and severe respiratory distress. What should the nurse do first?
o: Remove any object embedded in the chest.
Offer oral fluids.
Delay assessment until imaging is completed.
Activate emergency response and support airway and breathing while applying oxygen per protocol.
r: Penetrating chest trauma can rapidly impair ventilation and circulation. Stabilization and emergency response precede diagnostic imaging.

q: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax has unilateral decreased breath sounds but stable vital signs. What is the appropriate nursing action?
o: Continue close respiratory monitoring and promptly notify the clinician for evaluation.
Dismiss the finding because stable blood pressure excludes pneumothorax.
Encourage vigorous exercise.
Perform needle decompression independently without an order or protocol.
r: Unilateral decreased breath sounds can reflect pneumothorax even before instability; timely evaluation and monitoring are appropriate.

q: A patient with flail chest reports severe pain and shallow breathing. What nursing approach best supports ventilation?
o: Restrict all analgesia so respiratory rate remains high.
Promptly address pain using the prescribed plan and encourage coached breathing as tolerated.
Bind the chest tightly to immobilize the segment.
Ask the patient to avoid coughing and deep breathing entirely.
r: Pain limits ventilation and secretion clearance. Appropriate analgesia and coached respiratory care support breathing; tight binding can worsen mechanics.

q: A nurse is caring for a patient after thoracic trauma. Which trend most strongly suggests worsening respiratory compromise?
o: Stable effort and improving oxygen saturation.
Mild bruising with unchanged respiratory findings.
Increasing work of breathing with falling oxygen saturation and new confusion.
Improved alertness and warm skin.
r: Rising work of breathing, hypoxemia, and mental-status change indicate deteriorating oxygenation and require immediate reassessment.

q: A patient with a chest injury has tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, and hypotension. What should the nurse suspect?
o: An uncomplicated rib contusion.
A stable isolated pleural effusion.
A normal response to pain.
Tension pneumothorax with obstructed venous return.
r: These findings can occur in tension pneumothorax, where rising intrathoracic pressure compromises ventilation and venous return; emergency intervention is needed.

q: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax asks why the clinician ordered chest imaging. Which response is best?
o: “Imaging helps assess the pleural space and lung expansion, while your symptoms and vital signs guide urgency.”
“A normal image would make respiratory assessment unnecessary.”
“Imaging measures only the heart’s electrical activity.”
“Imaging immediately treats the collapsed lung.”
r: Imaging supports diagnosis and extent assessment, but it does not replace ongoing clinical monitoring or treatment.

q: A postoperative patient suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and severe dyspnea. What should the nurse do first?
o: Massage the calves to dislodge a possible clot.
Activate emergency support, assess oxygenation and circulation, and report suspected pulmonary embolism.
Encourage the patient to walk to relieve pain.
Wait for the next routine vital-sign check.
r: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain after surgery may indicate PE. Stabilize and escalate immediately; do not massage a suspected DVT.

q: A patient has unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. Which action should the nurse avoid?
o: Measuring and comparing both legs as directed.
Notifying the clinician for evaluation.
Massaging or vigorously manipulating the affected leg.
Assessing for chest pain or dyspnea.
r: Manipulation can potentially dislodge thrombus. Assess and escalate suspected DVT without massage.

q: A patient receiving anticoagulation for DVT reports blood in the urine. What should the nurse advise?
o: Take an extra dose to prevent clot extension.
Stop treatment permanently without notifying anyone.
Ignore the finding unless pain develops.
Contact the care team promptly for assessment of possible bleeding; seek urgent care for heavy bleeding or instability.
r: Hematuria may be anticoagulant-associated bleeding. Prompt clinician guidance is needed; severe or unstable bleeding is an emergency.

q: A patient at increased VTE risk is beginning postoperative recovery. Which action helps reduce venous stasis when safe and prescribed?
o: Early mobilization and use of ordered mechanical prophylaxis.
Keeping the patient immobile for several days.
Applying tight bands behind the knees.
Massaging both legs every hour.
r: Early movement and prescribed compression strategies reduce venous stasis; avoid constricting bands and massage.

q: A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism becomes hypotensive and increasingly confused. Which priority is appropriate?
o: A routine outpatient referral.
Rapid emergency escalation with airway, breathing, and circulation support.
A long walk to improve circulation.
Oral fluids followed by discharge.
r: Hypotension and altered mentation suggest high-risk PE with impaired perfusion. Emergency stabilization is required.

q: A patient taking an anticoagulant for a pulmonary embolism asks about using a new herbal supplement. What should the nurse say?
o: All supplements are safe because they are natural.
Stop the anticoagulant while using the supplement.
Check with the prescriber or pharmacist before starting it because supplements can interact with anticoagulants.
Take both at double strength.
r: Herbal products may alter bleeding risk or drug effect. Medication reconciliation with a clinician/pharmacist is safest.

q: A patient with a confirmed DVT asks why the nurse discourages crossing the legs for long periods. Which response is best?
o: “Crossing your legs always breaks the clot apart.”
“Position has no effect on venous circulation.”
“You should stay completely still until the clot disappears.”
“Prolonged pressure and immobility can impede venous return; changing position and moving as directed helps circulation.”
r: Avoid prolonged immobility and follow prescribed activity guidance. Do not imply that a simple position will dislodge a clot.

q: A nurse is teaching a patient prescribed an anticoagulant. Which statement should prompt follow-up teaching?
o: “If I miss a dose, I will double the next one.”
“I will use the medication exactly as prescribed.”
“I will report unusual bruising or bleeding.”
“I will tell clinicians and dentists that I take this medicine.”
r: Doubling a missed dose may cause harm; missed-dose instructions vary by drug and should come from the care team or official medication guidance.

q: A patient with a prior DVT reports sudden shortness of breath and near-syncope at home. Which instruction is safest?
o: Schedule a routine clinic visit next month.
Call emergency services now; do not drive yourself.
Take a family member’s anticoagulant.
Lie down and wait several hours before seeking help.
r: Sudden dyspnea and presyncope may indicate PE and require emergency assessment; driving while unstable is unsafe.

q: A patient returns after a long trip with unilateral leg swelling. Which additional symptom most increases concern for PE?
o: A mild headache that resolved.
Chronic unchanged knee stiffness.
New unexplained shortness of breath.
A small bruise on the opposite arm.
r: New dyspnea accompanying a possible DVT raises concern that thrombus has embolized to the lungs.

q: A hospitalized patient has an order for sequential compression devices but reports new calf pain and swelling. What should the nurse do?
o: Apply the device more tightly over the painful area.
Massage the calf before putting on the device.
Ignore the symptom and continue without assessment.
Pause applying the device to the affected leg and urgently notify the clinician for DVT evaluation.
r: New unilateral pain and swelling require evaluation for DVT before compression is applied to that extremity, according to clinical direction.

q: A patient on anticoagulation falls and strikes their head but feels well. What should the nurse advise?
o: Seek immediate medical evaluation because bleeding may occur even without early symptoms.
Wait for a severe headache before calling.
Skip the next several doses without contacting the prescriber.
Take aspirin for soreness.
r: Head injury during anticoagulation warrants urgent evaluation for internal bleeding; do not self-adjust therapy or add antiplatelets.

q: A patient with PE is receiving oxygen and monitoring. Which change should the nurse report immediately?
o: Stable breathing on the ordered oxygen.
Worsening oxygenation, new hypotension, or altered mental status.
Improved chest discomfort and stable vital signs.
A request for a blanket.
r: These changes can indicate worsening gas exchange or hemodynamic compromise from PE and require rapid escalation.

q: A patient asks whether compression stockings replace anticoagulant treatment for a diagnosed DVT. What is the best response?
o: “Yes, stockings dissolve any clot.”
“Stop all medicines once stockings are applied.”
“No. Follow the prescribed treatment plan; compression may be used for selected reasons but does not replace anticoagulation when it is indicated.”
“Wear any size as tightly as possible.”
r: Compression does not substitute for indicated anticoagulation. Treatment is individualized, and garments must fit and be used as directed.

q: A patient with worsening respiratory failure is drowsy, using accessory muscles, and has falling oxygen saturation despite prescribed oxygen. What is the priority?
o: Turn off oxygen to see whether the saturation improves.
Offer food and encourage sleep.
Wait for the next scheduled arterial blood gas.
Escalate immediately for airway/ventilatory support and reassess oxygenation.
r: Mental-status decline and increased work of breathing despite oxygen can signal impending respiratory failure; urgent escalation is essential.

q: A patient with chronic lung disease becomes increasingly confused and has shallow respirations. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, and ventilation; promptly notify the clinician.
Assume the confusion is baseline without checking.
Give sedatives to reduce anxiety before assessment.
Encourage the patient to lie flat.
r: Confusion and shallow breathing may reflect hypoxemia or hypercapnia. Immediate respiratory assessment and escalation are needed.

q: A patient with respiratory failure is being considered for noninvasive ventilation. Which finding should be communicated as a potential concern?
o: Alertness and ability to cooperate with the mask.
Inability to protect the airway or manage secretions.
A stable blood pressure and intact cough.
Understanding how to call for help.
r: Noninvasive ventilation requires a patient able to protect the airway and tolerate the interface; inability to do so may require another airway strategy.

q: A patient on oxygen has an unexpectedly low pulse-oximeter reading but is alert and speaking comfortably. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase oxygen to maximum without assessment or order.
Document the number as accurate and leave the room.
Assess the patient and verify the signal, probe placement, and reading while checking for respiratory distress.
Remove the probe and stop monitoring.
r: Pulse oximetry can be affected by signal quality and perfusion. Correlate the value with the patient and verify promptly without ignoring risk.

q: A patient with heart failure and a history of valve disease suddenly develops chest pressure, diaphoresis, and hypotension. What is the nurse’s priority?
o: Complete routine intake documentation first.
Encourage the patient to walk to improve cardiac output.
Wait for a scheduled echocardiogram.
Activate emergency cardiac support and assess airway, breathing, circulation, and rhythm.
r: Acute chest pain with hypotension suggests possible ischemia and shock. Stabilization and emergency escalation take precedence.

q: A patient with a cardiac diagnosis has new edema, rising daily weight, and worsening exertional dyspnea. Which response is best?
o: Assess for fluid overload and notify the clinician so the treatment plan can be reviewed.
Recommend a high-sodium diet and no follow-up.
Advise the patient to double a diuretic without an order.
Treat each symptom as unrelated to the heart.
r: The combined trend suggests worsening congestion. Assessment and clinician review are needed; medication adjustment must be prescribed.

q: A patient with a chest tube after a pulmonary embolism workup becomes acutely restless, tachypneic, and cyanotic. What should the nurse do?
o: Focus only on the previous imaging report.
Call for emergency help and rapidly assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, and chest-drain function.
Ask the patient to ambulate to improve oxygenation.
Wait until the next scheduled respiratory treatment.
r: Restlessness, tachypnea, and cyanosis signal severe hypoxemia. Immediate respiratory support and evaluation of the drain and underlying cause are necessary.

q: A patient with a rapid irregular rhythm suddenly loses consciousness and has no palpable pulse. What should the nurse do?
o: Attempt a vagal maneuver.
Wait for a 12-lead ECG before starting CPR.
Begin CPR and activate the pulseless-arrest response; use the rhythm-based algorithm.
Give oral anticoagulation.
r: A pulseless patient is in cardiac arrest regardless of prior rhythm. CPR and emergency algorithm-based resuscitation must start immediately.

q: A patient with mitral valve disease and atrial fibrillation suddenly reports weakness and cannot move the right arm. What is the priority action?
o: Give food and reassess arm strength later.
Wait for the scheduled cardiology appointment.
Assume the weakness is a harmless medication effect.
Activate stroke response, determine last-known-well time, and maintain emergency monitoring.
r: Atrial fibrillation increases embolic stroke risk. New unilateral weakness demands immediate stroke evaluation and last-known-well documentation.
